summary.text: A mantle plume is a proposed kind of mantle convection in which super-heated material forms at the core-mantle boundary and rises, put forward to explain anomalous volcanism.
Plumes are often invoked as the cause of hotspots such as Hawaii and Iceland and of large igneous provinces such as the Deccan and Siberian Traps.
As a plate moves over a fixed plume, eruptions are expected to build a chain of volcanoes parallel to the plate's motion, with the Hawaiian Islands as the classic case.

facts.label: Shape
facts.value: Like a mushroom: thin conduit, bulbous head

items.prompt: Laboratory tank experiments suggest what overall form a rising plume takes?

options.label: A flat, spreading pancake
A twisting corkscrew
A mushroom with a thin stalk
A string of equal-sized beads

items.explain: Experiments suggest a plume has a long thin conduit topped by a bulbous head, so the whole structure resembles a mushroom.

items.prompt: Why does a rising plume develop a swollen head on top of its narrow conduit?

options.label: Hot material flows up the conduit faster than the plume rises
The top cools and puffs up as it nears the crust
The surrounding mantle squeezes the conduit flat
The core pulls the base of the plume back down

items.explain: The bulbous head forms because hot material moves up the conduit faster than the plume itself rises through its surroundings.

items.prompt: A tectonic plate slides steadily over a plume that stays in one place. What pattern of volcanoes should appear on the plate?

options.label: A ring around the plume
A chain lined up with the plate's motion
One volcano that keeps growing
A chain at right angles to the plate's motion

items.explain: As the plate moves over a fixed hotspot, eruptions are expected to form a chain of volcanoes that parallels the plate's motion.

items.prompt: Along a hotspot chain like Hawaii's, where would you expect to find the oldest volcanoes?

options.label: Directly above the active hotspot
Scattered at random along the chain
Exactly in the middle of the chain
At the far end, away from the hotspot

items.explain: Hotspots such as Hawaii's have time-progressive chains of older volcanoes extending out from them, so age increases with distance from the hotspot.

items.prompt: When a plume head reaches the base of the lithosphere, what is it expected to do?

options.label: Punch straight through as a narrow jet
Freeze into a solid plug
Sink back toward the core
Flatten out and melt into lots of basalt magma

items.explain: The head is expected to flatten against the lithosphere and undergo widespread decompression melting, forming large volumes of basalt magma that may then erupt.

items.prompt: Hotspot lavas carry chemical traces of near-surface material such as old subducted slabs. How does the plume idea explain this?

options.label: The slabs never sank and were simply re-melted
Meteorite impacts mixed the material into the lava
Slabs sank to the core-mantle boundary and plumes brought them back
The material stayed in the shallow mantle the whole time

items.explain: In the plume view, subducting slabs carried near-surface material down to the core-mantle boundary, and plumes carried it back up to the surface.
